opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, because AlphaFold 3 was a real step change, but it's only one piece of what you need to actually design a drug.

What AlphaFold 3 does really well is give you a static picture: here's the protein, here's how a small molecule or another protein might sit in it, here's the structure of that complex. That's hugely valuable. But drug design isn't just a structure problem. Biology is dynamic. Proteins move, they flex, they have multiple conformations, and often the most interesting therapeutic opportunities live in those transient states. A single snapshot doesn't capture that.

The second gap is going from structure to the properties you actually care about. Knowing a molecule *can* bind somewhere is different from knowing how tightly it binds, how selective it is against all the related proteins in the body, whether it's soluble, whether it gets metabolized in the liver, whether it's toxic. Those are the things that make or break a drug program, and a structure prediction model on its own doesn't give you reliable answers there.

Third, AlphaFold 3 is fundamentally a predictive model. You give it an input and it tells you what that system looks like. Drug design is the inverse problem: I want a molecule with these properties, what is it? So you need generative systems that can search that enormous chemical space and propose candidates, and then models accurate enough to score them so you're not burning months in the wet lab on dead ends.

So the way I think about it is that AlphaFold 3 is a foundational building block. What we really want is a whole stack of models, covering structure, dynamics, binding affinity, and ADMET properties, all working together inside a design loop. The goal is to be able to do most of the drug discovery process in silico, with much higher confidence, and only go to the lab to confirm. That's the bigger vision, and we're still a fair way from it.

r001.rationale: It says that knowing a molecule can bind is different from knowing how tightly it binds, identifying binding strength as a needed capability.

r002.rationale: It describes proteins moving among conformations, but does not identify how a molecule’s interaction changes a protein’s conformation.

r003.rationale: It does not connect changes in protein conformation to effects on protein function.

r004.rationale: It discusses protein dynamics generally, but does not identify effects of molecular interactions on cellular dynamics.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should say up front, I think AlphaFold 3 is a genuinely remarkable piece of work, and I was lucky enough to be around for a lot of the journey that led to it. So none of this is a criticism of what it is. It's more about what it isn't, and what the actual problem of drug design demands.

The first thing is that AlphaFold 3 gives you a structure. It gives you a static snapshot of how a protein and a ligand might sit together. But proteins aren't static objects. They breathe, they flex, they have ensembles of conformations, and a lot of what makes a drug work or fail is dynamic. Is this pocket actually open long enough for the molecule to get in? Does binding stabilise one state over another? A single predicted pose doesn't tell you that.

The second is that structure is a means to an end, not the end. What a medicinal chemist actually cares about is: does this molecule bind tightly, is it selective against the fifty other kinases that look nearly identical, is it soluble, is it going to get metabolised by the liver in ten minutes, is it toxic? AlphaFold 3 is answering one piece of that puzzle, and arguably not even the piece that kills most programs. Most drugs don't fail because we couldn't figure out the binding pose. They fail on potency, selectivity, ADME, and ultimately on whether the biology was right in the first place.

And then the third thing, and this is the one I find most interesting, is that AlphaFold 3 is a predictor, not a designer. You give it inputs and it tells you what probably happens. Drug design is a generative, iterative, search problem. You're navigating an enormous chemical space, making a molecule, measuring it, learning something, and deciding what to make next. The models we need have to live inside that loop. They need to propose, be wrong, get corrected by real experimental data, and get better. That's a very different kind of system from a model that's trained once on the PDB and then queried.

And that leads to the data point, which is maybe the deepest limitation. AlphaFold worked because there were decades of crystallographers depositing structures into a public database. There is no equivalent for the questions that actually matter in drug design. There's no public database of a hundred million clean, consistent binding affinity measurements across chemical space. That data either doesn't exist or it's locked up inside pharma companies, collected under inconsistent conditions. So you can't just scale your way out of it with a bigger model. You have to think about how you generate the right data, which means wet lab experimentation that's actually designed to teach the model.

So the way I'd put it is, AlphaFold 3 is a beautiful proof that these systems can learn the physics of molecular interactions from data. What I want is to take that lesson and apply it to the whole pipeline, with models that are embedded in a loop with real experiments, so that the thing that improves over time isn't just the structure predictor, it's the entire process of discovering a medicine.

r001.rationale: The response says medicinal chemists need to know whether a molecule binds tightly and identifies potency as a limitation beyond AlphaFold 3’s structural prediction.

r002.rationale: It asks whether binding stabilizes one protein state over another, directly identifying how the interaction can change the protein’s conformation.

r003.rationale: The response discusses protein conformations but does not identify how those conformational changes affect protein function.

r004.rationale: It does not identify effects of protein interactions on cellular dynamics.

astra-6.text:
I think AlphaFold 3 is a remarkable step forward, but predicting a structure is only one part of designing a drug. It helps answer, “What might these molecules look like when they interact?” What we ultimately want to ask is, “What molecule should I make to produce a particular effect?” Those are quite different questions.

A plausible binding pose doesn’t necessarily tell you how strongly a molecule binds, whether it’s selective, or whether it will have the effect you want in a cell. And then there are all the other properties that make something a medicine: can it reach the right tissue, is it safe, can you manufacture it?

So what I want AI to enable is a design process across all of those requirements, with experiments feeding back into the models. You generate a molecule, make it, test it, and use what you learn to improve the next design. Structure prediction is a powerful component of that, but the ambition is to move from predicting what biology looks like to designing molecules that reliably change what biology does.

r001.rationale: It says a plausible binding pose does not tell you how strongly a molecule binds, identifying binding-strength prediction as a needed capability.

r002.rationale: It does not identify predicting interaction-driven changes in a protein’s conformation.

r003.rationale: It does not connect protein conformational changes to effects on protein function.

r004.rationale: It mentions whether a molecule has a desired effect in a cell, but does not identify predicting how protein interactions affect cellular dynamics.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AlphaFold 3 is an incredible step forward, but predicting a structure is only one part of designing a drug. What you really want to know is: if I make this molecule, will it have the effect I want? Will it bind strongly enough and selectively enough? Can it get to the right place in the body? And will it be safe?

A predicted structure can help you reason about some of those questions, but it doesn’t answer them directly. Biology is dynamic, and a picture of a molecular interaction doesn’t tell you the whole story of what happens in a cell or a patient.

So what I want AI to enable is a much more complete design loop: generate a molecule, predict the properties that matter, test it experimentally, and use those results to improve the next design. AlphaFold 3 is a powerful component of that. The broader challenge is turning that understanding into molecules that actually work as medicines.

r002.rationale: It does not describe predicting how a protein’s conformation changes during molecular interaction.

r003.rationale: It does not connect protein conformational changes to effects on protein function.

r004.rationale: It says biology is dynamic and that a molecular picture does not explain what happens in a cell, but does not identify predicting how protein interactions affect cellular dynamics as a needed capability.
